newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cancer panel advises mammograms in 40s.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cancer panel advises mammograms in 40s.

text.p: U.S. National Cancer Institute advisers on Thursday formally recommended that women in their 40s get mammograms every year or two if they are at average risk for breast cancer.
The National Cancer Advisory Board made the unequivocal recommendation after years of increasingly acrimonious debate about the the value of mammograms for women under age 50.
Dr Richard Klausner, director of the federal National Cancer Institute, has said he would follow the board's advice.

"We've known for quite some time that screening mammography is capable of saving lives, of reducing mortality," Klausner said at a news conference where the new recommendations were announced. "The question that has been difficult to resolve is when women should begin regular screening mammography."
Until 1993, the NCI did recommend regular breast X-rays for women in their 40s, but it dropped the recommendation that year because the available data did not show that the testing was saving lives.
Other medical groups, including the privately funded American Cancer Society, continued to advise women under 50 to have the screening and NCI took a second look at the issue this year.
Dr Barbara Rimer, head of the advisory board, noted that women's risk of developing breast cancer varies, but also cited the potential benefits of early detection.

"The benefit of mammography is detection of cancer early when it is more easily treated with a better outcome," Rimer said. "Regular screening mammography in average-risk women ages 40-49 reduces deaths from breast cancer by about 17 percent. By early detection of breast cancer, treatment is not only more effective but potentially less disfiguring and toxic."
She also noted the limitations of mammography, especially false positive results, and said the board's recommendations could change in the future as more studies are conducted.

The advisory board said women who are at higher risk for breast cancer should seek medical advice about whether they should have mammograms before they turn 40 and about how often they should have the tests in their 40s.

There has been no controversy about whether mammograms have life-saving benefits for women over age 50, and the advisory board repeated its recommendation that women over that age should have mammograms every one to two years.
